mcqs.stem: Best guess: which plaintiff can generally sue an accountant for fraud?

choices.text: Only the client that engaged the accountant
Any foreseeable third party who relied on it
choices.explanation: Correct. Fraud liability extends to all reasonably foreseeable third parties who relied.

choices.text: Only parties in privity of contract
choices.explanation: Privity matters for negligence under Ultramares.

choices.text: Only the SEC, through an enforcement action

mcqs.explanation: Fraud liability extends to all reasonably foreseeable third parties who relied.

mcqs.stem: Under the Restatement (Second) §552 approach, which third party can sue an accountant for ordinary negligence?

choices.text: Any reasonably foreseeable user of the report
A limited class of users the accountant knew would rely
choices.explanation: Correct. The Restatement extends liability to foreseen users — a known, limited group.

choices.text: Only a party in privity of contract with the accountant
No third party; only the client may sue
choices.explanation: The Restatement allows some third parties.

mcqs.explanation: The Restatement extends liability to foreseen users — a known, limited group.

mcqs.stem: Under §11 of the 1933 Act, which must the plaintiff prove?

choices.text: The accountant's negligence in the audit
choices.explanation: Negligence needn't be proven; the accountant bears the burden of due diligence.

choices.text: A material misstatement or omission, and a loss
choices.explanation: Correct. §11 plaintiffs show a material misstatement and damages; the accountant can raise due diligence.

choices.text: Scienter on the part of the accountant
choices.explanation: Scienter is required under Rule 10b-5, not §11.

choices.text: Privity of contract with the accountant

mcqs.explanation: §11 plaintiffs show a material misstatement and damages; the accountant can raise due diligence.

mcqs.stem: Under the Ultramares rule, which party may sue an accountant for ordinary negligence?

choices.text: Any reasonably foreseeable user of the statements
Only the SEC, through enforcement actions
Any shareholder of the audit client
The client, and third parties in or near privity
choices.explanation: Correct. Ultramares limits negligence liability to parties in privity or near privity.

mcqs.explanation: Ultramares limits negligence liability to parties in privity or near privity.

mcqs.stem: Which is a defense available to an accountant sued under §11 of the 1933 Act?

choices.text: Due diligence: a reasonable investigation and belief
choices.explanation: Correct. §11 defenses: due diligence, the plaintiff knew of the misstatement, or the loss wasn't caused by it.

choices.text: Lack of privity with the plaintiff purchaser
The plaintiff didn't read the registration statement
The accountant was merely negligent, not reckless

mcqs.explanation: §11 defenses: due diligence, the plaintiff knew of the misstatement, or the loss wasn't caused by it.

mcqs.stem: To recover under Rule 10b-5, a plaintiff must prove the accountant acted with:

choices.text: Ordinary negligence in performing the audit
Privity of contract with the plaintiff
Scienter: intent to deceive or recklessness
choices.explanation: Correct. 10b-5 requires scienter, reliance, and damages.

choices.text: Strict liability for any misstatement

mcqs.explanation: 10b-5 requires scienter, reliance, and damages.

mcqs.stem: Who owns an accountant's working papers?

choices.text: The client that paid for the audit
choices.explanation: Working papers belong to the accountant.

choices.text: The state board of accountancy
The IRS, for tax-related work papers
The accountant, subject to confidentiality
choices.explanation: Correct. The accountant owns the working papers but must keep client information confidential.

mcqs.explanation: The accountant owns the working papers but must keep client information confidential.

mcqs.stem: Which communication is protected by the §7525 federal tax practitioner privilege?

choices.text: Tax advice in a criminal tax investigation
Audit working papers in a securities suit
Written communications promoting a tax shelter
Tax advice by a CPA in a noncriminal IRS proceeding
choices.explanation: Correct. §7525 extends a limited privilege to federally authorized tax practitioners in noncriminal tax matters.

mcqs.explanation: §7525 extends a limited privilege to federally authorized tax practitioners in noncriminal tax matters.

mcqs.stem: An auditor was negligent, but the client's own negligence contributed to its loss. In a comparative negligence state, what is the effect?

choices.text: The auditor pays nothing at all
choices.explanation: That's contributory negligence in some states.

choices.text: The auditor pays double the client's loss
choices.explanation: There's no basis for double damages.

choices.text: Damages are cut in proportion to the client's fault
choices.explanation: Correct. Comparative negligence apportions damages; pure contributory negligence (a minority rule) can bar recovery.

choices.text: The client's own fault is irrelevant to damages

mcqs.explanation: Comparative negligence apportions damages; pure contributory negligence (a minority rule) can bar recovery.

mcqs.stem: An auditor recklessly ignored obvious red flags but didn't intend to deceive. Which liability most likely applies to foreseeable third parties?

choices.text: Gross negligence (constructive fraud)
choices.explanation: Correct. Reckless disregard (constructive fraud) extends liability to foreseeable third parties.

choices.text: None, because there was no intent to deceive
Breach of contract with the client only
choices.explanation: Third parties aren't parties to the contract.

choices.text: Strict liability to all users

mcqs.explanation: Reckless disregard (constructive fraud) extends liability to foreseeable third parties.

mcqs.stem: Under §18 of the 1934 Act, what defense can an accountant raise?

choices.text: Good faith and no knowledge that it was false
choices.explanation: Correct. §18 covers false or misleading filings with the SEC; the plaintiff must prove reliance, and good faith is a defense.

choices.text: Lack of privity with the plaintiff
That the filing was voluntary, not required
Due diligence, as under the 1933 Act

mcqs.explanation: §18 covers false or misleading filings with the SEC; the plaintiff must prove reliance, and good faith is a defense.

mcqs.stem: A client sues its CPA for failing to complete a tax return by the agreed date, causing penalties. What claim fits best?

choices.text: Breach of contract
choices.explanation: Correct. Failure to perform agreed services is a breach of contract (and possibly negligence).

choices.text: A Rule 10b-5 securities fraud claim
A §11 registration statement claim
Common-law fraud and deceit

mcqs.explanation: Failure to perform agreed services is a breach of contract (and possibly negligence).

mcqs.stem: Which element is required for any negligence claim?

choices.text: Intent to deceive the plaintiff
choices.explanation: Intent is an element of fraud, not negligence.

choices.text: Privity of contract, in every state
A misstatement in a registration statement
Proximate cause linking breach and damages
choices.explanation: Correct. Negligence: duty, breach, proximate cause, and damages.

mcqs.explanation: Negligence: duty, breach, proximate cause, and damages.

mcqs.stem: A client tells its CPA that the audited statements will be given to First Bank for a loan. The CPA is negligent, and First Bank relies on the statements and suffers a loss. Under the Restatement approach, can First Bank recover?

choices.text: Yes, as a known, foreseen user
choices.explanation: Correct. The Restatement extends negligence liability to a limited class of foreseen users.

choices.text: No, because it lacks privity
Only if the CPA acted with scienter
Only if the bank paid the fee

mcqs.explanation: Restatement (Second) of Torts §552: an accountant is liable for negligence to the limited group of persons the accountant knows will rely on the information.

mcqs.stem: Which approach lets any reasonably foreseeable user recover from an accountant for ordinary negligence?

choices.text: The Ultramares (privity) approach
The foreseeability (Rosenblum) approach
choices.explanation: Correct. It is the broadest approach.

choices.text: The Restatement approach
choices.explanation: It is limited to foreseen users.

choices.text: The Credit Alliance approach

mcqs.explanation: Under the Rosenblum foreseeability approach, accountants are liable for negligence to all reasonably foreseeable users.

mcqs.stem: Which element distinguishes a fraud claim against an accountant from a negligence claim?

choices.text: Damages
A duty of care
Scienter
choices.explanation: Correct. Fraud requires knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard.

choices.text: Causation

mcqs.explanation: Fraud requires scienter: intent to deceive or knowledge of falsity (or reckless disregard). Negligence doesn't.

mcqs.stem: A client sues its CPA for breach of contract for not finishing the engagement. Which defense is available to the CPA?

choices.text: The CPA followed all of GAAS
The client is a public company
choices.explanation: Not relevant to the contract claim.

choices.text: No written engagement letter was signed
The client withheld needed records
choices.explanation: Correct. A party's own interference excuses performance.

mcqs.explanation: A client's failure to cooperate or provide records prevents performance and is a defense to a breach-of-contract claim.

mcqs.stem: An auditor fully complied with GAAS, yet the statements turned out to be misleading. How does GAAS compliance affect a negligence claim?

choices.text: It's evidence, not a complete defense
choices.explanation: Correct. A court may still find a lack of due care.

choices.text: It's an absolute defense to the claim
It's irrelevant to the negligence claim
choices.explanation: It is evidence of due care.

choices.text: It shifts all liability to the client

mcqs.explanation: Compliance with professional standards is persuasive evidence of due care but doesn't conclusively bar a negligence finding.

mcqs.stem: When may a CPA disclose confidential client information without the client's consent?

choices.text: When a client's competitor asks
In response to a valid subpoena
choices.explanation: Correct. Compliance with a subpoena or summons is permitted.

choices.text: When selling the practice's goodwill
choices.explanation: Consent is still needed for files.

choices.text: When a lender asks informally

mcqs.explanation: A CPA may disclose confidential information without consent to comply with a validly issued subpoena or summons.

mcqs.stem: Does the §7525 federally authorized tax practitioner privilege apply in a criminal tax proceeding?

choices.text: Yes, in all federal proceedings
choices.explanation: It is limited to noncriminal matters.

choices.text: Yes, if the client is an individual
No
choices.explanation: Correct. It covers only noncriminal tax matters.

choices.text: Only in state court

mcqs.explanation: §7525 applies only to noncriminal tax matters before the IRS and in federal courts, and not to written tax shelter promotion.

mcqs.stem: During a compilation, a CPA notices invoices suggesting an employee is embezzling but says nothing. Later the losses grow. What is the CPA's exposure?

choices.text: None, because a compilation isn't an audit
Liability only to the client's bank
Criminal liability for the employee's theft
choices.explanation: The CPA didn't commit the theft.

choices.text: Negligence for not telling the client
choices.explanation: Correct. The CPA must communicate known indications of fraud.

mcqs.explanation: Even in a compilation, a CPA who becomes aware of indications of fraud must communicate them; failing to do so can be negligent.

mcqs.stem: A CPA materially breaches an engagement by never delivering the agreed report. Can the CPA recover its fee?

choices.text: No, not after a material breach
choices.explanation: Correct. A material breach bars recovery of the fee.

choices.text: Yes, the full agreed fee in every case
choices.explanation: A material breach bars the fee.

choices.text: Yes, for all hours actually worked
Only if the client suffered no loss

mcqs.explanation: A party that materially breaches a contract generally can't recover the contract price; minor breaches allow recovery less damages.

mcqs.stem: A client engages a CPA to audit its statements specifically so they can be given to a named lender. The CPA is negligent. Under Ultramares, can the lender sue for negligence?

choices.text: No, it lacks privity with the CPA
Yes, as a primary beneficiary
Only for fraud, not negligence
Only if it paid part of the fee

mcqs.explanation: Under Ultramares, a third-party primary beneficiary known to the accountant may sue for ordinary negligence.

mcqs.stem: A CPA negligently fails to file a client's return on time. What can the client recover from the CPA?

choices.text: The tax owed on the return
choices.explanation: The tax would have been owed anyway.

choices.text: Punitive damages for negligence
The penalties caused by the delay
choices.explanation: Correct. The tax itself was owed anyway.

choices.text: Nothing, as returns are the client's duty

mcqs.explanation: Damages for negligent tax preparation compensate for harm caused, such as penalties, not the underlying tax.

mcqs.stem: A CPA recklessly disregarded obvious problems in an audit. Under Ultramares, can an unknown but foreseeable investor recover?

choices.text: No, only clients may sue
Only if named in the engagement letter
No, reckless conduct isn't actionable
Yes, for gross negligence (constructive fraud)
choices.explanation: Correct. Privity isn't required for fraud-type claims.

mcqs.explanation: Gross negligence (constructive fraud) exposes accountants to liability to all reasonably foreseeable users, even in privity states.

mcqs.stem: In a negligence suit, what type of damages can a client ordinarily recover from its CPA?

choices.text: Compensatory damages
choices.explanation: Correct. Punitive damages require fraud-type conduct.

choices.text: Punitive damages
Treble damages
Only nominal damages

mcqs.explanation: Ordinary negligence supports compensatory damages; punitive damages generally require fraud or similar conduct.

mcqs.stem: A client suffers $500,000 of losses from its CPA's negligence. In a comparative negligence state, a jury finds the client 30% at fault. What can the client recover?

choices.explanation: Correct. Damages are reduced by the client's share of fault.

mcqs.explanation: Under comparative negligence, recovery is reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault.

mcqs.stem: An auditor followed GAAS, but a controller's collusive, well-concealed embezzlement went undetected. The client sues for negligence. What is the likely result?

choices.text: Liability for the full loss
No liability if due care was exercised
choices.explanation: Correct. An audit isn't a guarantee against collusive fraud.

choices.text: Automatic liability for any fraud
Liability only for the audit fee

mcqs.explanation: Accountants are liable for negligence only if they failed to exercise due professional care.

mcqs.stem: An investor with no relationship to the CPA proves the CPA knew the audited statements were materially false. Can the investor recover?

choices.text: No, for lack of privity
Only under the Restatement
Yes, for fraud
choices.explanation: Correct. Fraud liability extends to all foreseeable users.

choices.text: Only if named in the report

mcqs.explanation: Actual fraud exposes the accountant to all reasonably foreseeable third parties who relied.

mcqs.stem: A CPA delivers a client's review report a month late, and the client loses a loan it had told the CPA depended on timely delivery. What may the client recover?

choices.text: Only a refund of the fee
Punitive damages for delay
Nothing; reports are often late
Foreseeable losses
choices.explanation: Correct. The CPA knew the deadline mattered.

mcqs.explanation: Breach of contract damages include losses the parties could foresee when contracting.

mcqs.stem: A client tells its CPA the audit is for loans from "several regional banks" without naming them. A regional bank relies on the negligent audit. Under the Restatement, can it recover?

choices.text: Yes, as part of a foreseen class
choices.explanation: Correct. The class needn't be identified by name.

choices.text: No, because it wasn't named
Only under the Ultramares rule
Only if it proves fraud

mcqs.explanation: Restatement §552 covers a limited group the accountant knows will rely, even if individual members aren't named.

mcqs.stem: An auditor signs an unmodified opinion without ever observing the material inventory or performing alternatives. An unknown investor relies on it. What claim is strongest?

choices.text: Ordinary negligence
Constructive fraud
choices.explanation: Correct. Reckless disregard extends liability to foreseeable users.

choices.text: Breach of contract
No claim at all

mcqs.explanation: Gross negligence amounting to reckless disregard is treated as constructive fraud.

mcqs.stem: A state recognizes an accountant-client privilege. In a federal tax evasion prosecution, must the CPA testify about client communications?

choices.text: No, the state privilege applies
choices.explanation: State privilege doesn't bind federal courts.

choices.text: No, §7525 protects them
Yes, no privilege applies
choices.explanation: Correct. Federal courts don't recognize the state privilege, and §7525 excludes criminal matters.

choices.text: Only with the client's consent

mcqs.explanation: There's no federal common-law accountant-client privilege, and §7525 doesn't cover criminal proceedings.

mcqs.stem: A jury finds a CPA committed fraud that harmed investors. Which damages may be available beyond compensatory damages?

choices.text: Treble damages under common law
No further damages
Only the audit fee
Punitive damages for delay
choices.explanation: Correct. Fraud can support punitive awards.

mcqs.explanation: Punitive damages may be awarded for intentional misconduct such as fraud.

mcqs.stem: A plaintiff sues a CPA for negligence but admits it never read the audited statements before investing. What defense is strongest?

choices.text: No reliance
choices.explanation: Correct. The loss wasn't caused by the statements.

choices.text: Contributory negligence
The statute of frauds
Lack of consideration

mcqs.explanation: A plaintiff who didn't rely on the statements can't show the negligence caused its loss.

mcqs.stem: A CPA engaged only to prepare tax returns sees no signs of fraud and fails to detect an employee's embezzlement. Is the CPA liable?

choices.text: Yes, CPAs must always detect fraud
No, it wasn't within the engagement
choices.explanation: Correct. Absent known indications, tax work doesn't include fraud detection.

choices.text: Yes, under strict liability
Only if the loss is material

mcqs.explanation: A CPA's duty is defined by the engagement; there's no duty to detect fraud outside its scope unless aware of indications.

mcqs.stem: Under the Ultramares doctrine, to whom is an accountant liable for ordinary negligence?

choices.text: Parties in privity or near privity
choices.explanation: Correct. Ultramares limits negligence liability to privity.

choices.text: All reasonably foreseeable users
Any member of the investing public
Only the SEC and state regulators

mcqs.explanation: Ultramares restricts liability for ordinary negligence to those in privity or near privity with the accountant.

mcqs.stem: Which elements must a purchaser prove in a Section 11 (1933 Act) claim against an auditor?

choices.text: Reliance on the audited statements
A material misstatement and a loss
choices.explanation: Correct. Reliance and scienter aren't required.

choices.text: Scienter on the auditor's part
Privity of contract with the auditor

mcqs.explanation: Under Section 11, purchasers must show a material misstatement or omission in the registration statement and damages.

mcqs.stem: Under the Restatement (Second) of Torts approach used in most states, an accountant is liable for negligence to whom?

choices.text: All reasonably foreseeable users
The client and no one else
Known and intended users
choices.explanation: Correct. Restatement §552 extends to foreseen users.

choices.text: Only parties named in the contract

mcqs.explanation: The Restatement approach extends negligence liability to a limited group of users the accountant knows will rely on the work.

mcqs.stem: Under the Ultramares approach, a lender unknown to the auditor sues for negligence. What is the likely result?

choices.text: The lender recovers, because it was a foreseeable user
The auditor is strictly liable to the lender
The lender recovers under §11 of the 1933 Act
No recovery for ordinary negligence without near privity
choices.explanation: Correct. Ultramares limits negligence liability to parties in privity or near privity.

mcqs.explanation: Ultramares limits negligence liability to parties in privity or near privity.

mcqs.stem: Which must a plaintiff prove to recover from an auditor under Rule 10b-5?

choices.text: Scienter, reliance, and damages, plus a misstatement
choices.explanation: Correct. 10b-5 elements: material misstatement or omission, scienter, reliance, causation, and damages.

choices.text: Only a material misstatement in the statements
choices.explanation: Scienter, reliance, and damages are also required.

choices.text: Privity of contract with the auditor
Ordinary negligence by the auditor

mcqs.explanation: 10b-5 elements: material misstatement or omission, scienter, reliance, causation, and damages.

mcqs.stem: The IRC §7525 privilege for communications with a federally authorized tax practitioner applies to:

choices.text: Any communication in a criminal tax prosecution
choices.explanation: The privilege doesn't apply to criminal matters.

choices.text: Tax advice in a noncriminal IRS matter
choices.explanation: Correct. The privilege covers noncriminal tax matters before the IRS or in federal court.

choices.text: Written communications promoting a tax shelter
All work papers prepared for a financial audit

mcqs.explanation: §7525 extends attorney-client-type confidentiality to tax advice from federally authorized practitioners in noncriminal tax matters, excluding written tax shelter communications.

mcqs.stem: Under the Restatement (Second) of Torts approach, a CPA who negligently prepares financial statements is liable to:

choices.text: Only the client, under the strict privity rule
choices.explanation: That is the Ultramares rule, followed by fewer states.

choices.text: Third parties the CPA knew would rely on them
choices.explanation: Correct. Liability extends to a limited group of intended or known users.

choices.text: Anyone who could reasonably be foreseen to rely
choices.explanation: That is the broader foreseeability approach.

choices.text: No one, unless the CPA committed fraud
choices.explanation: Negligence liability exists to known users.

mcqs.explanation: The Restatement §552 approach extends negligence liability to a limited group of persons the accountant intends or knows will rely on the information.

flashcards.back: Ultramares (privity/near privity), Restatement §552 (foreseen users), foreseeability (foreseeable users).
A material misstatement in the registration statement and a loss; accountant's defense: due diligence.
Scienter (intent or recklessness), plus reliance and damages.
Federal tax advice in noncriminal matters; not tax shelter promotion.
